what_changed.headline: US policy remains inflation-dependent; Fed Governor Waller sees a hold if disinflation persists but would consider a September hike if August inflation reverses.
what_changed.significance: The next inflation data point is the key policy discriminator; growth and labor conditions are currently less binding.
what_changed.transmission: A hotter inflation outcome would raise expected policy rates and pressure duration-sensitive assets; continued disinflation would reduce that pressure.

what_changed.headline: Energy-related inflation risks remain elevated globally.
what_changed.significance: Renewed oil and European gas pressure may lift headline inflation and eventually challenge core-inflation assumptions.
what_changed.transmission: Higher energy costs can raise headline inflation, weaken real incomes and increase the probability of tighter monetary policy.

executive_decisions.development: Treat near-term duration exposure as conditional on incoming inflation data, not on labor-market weakness alone.
executive_decisions.why_it_matters: Waller describes inflation as the primary policy variable while characterizing activity and employment as broadly solid.
executive_decisions.transmission: Persistent inflation would keep front-end and long-end rate risks asymmetric; renewed disinflation would reopen easing optionality.

executive_decisions.development: Maintain a tactical rather than structural view on energy exposure.
executive_decisions.why_it_matters: Energy markets show physical tightness and positive carry, but futures are not unbiased forecasts and uncertainty is unusually high.
executive_decisions.transmission: Long exposure benefits from spot tightness and backwardation, but normalization of supply or curve structure would remove the carry support.

counterevidence.text: US July retail sales were weak, although the source attributes this partly to the timing of Amazon Prime Day.

regime_dashboard.state: Sticky with renewed energy upside risk

evidence.text: US PCE inflation was 3.7% year over year in July and core PCE was 3.3%; three-month core inflation was 3.05%.
Global core inflation has remained around 2.7% year over year, with core goods firming as services inflation moderates.
The Riksbank reported summer inflation above its June forecast but no clear evidence yet of a lasting broad inflation upturn.

counterevidence.text: US three-month core inflation has fallen from 4.76% in February, and Waller said wage growth adjusted for productivity is consistent with further disinflation.

Huw Pill argues the BoE should make an active policy choice rather than wait for geopolitical uncertainty to resolve, and prefers Bank Rate at 4%.

counterevidence.text: The Riksbank Governor said growth may improve without a significant near-term rise in inflationary pressure because labor-market slack remains.

evidence.text: Saxo reported US equities rebounding as yields stabilized, while European equities remained under pressure from elevated yields and Middle East tensions.

counterevidence.text: EM credit spreads were described as tight and range-bound, with no clear catalyst for a breakout.

evidence.text: A Stanford expert argued that the volume of government debt relative to GDP has risen substantially and that discretionary investors require more yield to absorb additional supply.
The same discussion reported that dealer balance sheets and Treasury-market liquidity measures were normal at the time considered.

evidence.text: The Treasury market discussion characterizes US government deficits and debt relative to GDP as high, with no clear end to the trend.
Morgan Stanley identifies a potential government shutdown risk in December and major fiscal debates around the NDAA.

macro_themes.thesis: Disinflation has improved in some measures, but sticky core inflation and renewed energy pressure leave central banks exposed to upside surprises.
macro_themes.market_implication: Rates remain highly data-sensitive; energy-sensitive currencies and inflation hedges may outperform if supply shocks persist, while duration benefits require cleaner inflation evidence.

observed_facts.text: US core PCE inflation was 3.3% year over year in July, while three-month core inflation had declined from February.
Global core inflation has been broadly unchanged around 2.7% year over year, with a rotation toward firmer core goods.

inferences.text: The combination of slowing services inflation and firmer goods and energy inflation could keep aggregate inflation above target for longer than a simple services-led disinflation narrative implies.
inferences.evidence_family: US PCE inflation; Global inflation monitor

unresolved_questions: Will August US inflation validate continued disinflation or trigger renewed tightening expectations?
Will energy pass-through into core inflation remain modest or intensify?

transmission.implication: Upside inflation surprises increase tightening risk and duration volatility.
Currencies of economies with credible tightening responses may gain relative support.
Persistent supply tightness supports energy prices and carry, subject to normalization risk.

catalysts: Further oil and European gas developments
invalidation_conditions: Several inflation releases show sustained broad-based disinflation despite energy pressure.

macro_themes.thesis: High public-debt issuance is interacting with finite dealer and investor balance-sheet capacity, keeping long-end term compensation structurally relevant.
macro_themes.market_implication: Long-duration rates may remain vulnerable even if near-term policy expectations soften; liquidity conditions should be monitored rather than assumed benign.

observed_facts.text: The Treasury-market discussion reports that the US government’s debt volume relative to GDP has continued to rise and that foreign official demand has not kept pace with the bond market’s expansion.
The Fed analysis finds Treasuries remain an important part of foreign official reserve portfolios, despite increased official gold accumulation.

inferences.text: Reserve diversification toward gold does not by itself establish a wholesale exit from Treasuries, but persistent issuance may still require higher compensation from marginal buyers.
inferences.evidence_family: Treasury market liquidity and intermediation; Foreign official reserve holdings

unresolved_questions: Can Treasury buybacks materially improve liquidity outside stressed conditions?
Will fiscal debates alter the expected path of issuance?

transmission.implication: Long-end yields may remain structurally sensitive to supply and term compensation.
Higher long-end yields can challenge valuation-sensitive growth sectors.
High core rates can pressure lower-rated issuers even if spreads remain contained.

catalysts: US fiscal negotiations and Treasury issuance policy
invalidation_conditions: A sustained decline in issuance pressure or clear improvement in intermediation capacity reduces long-end compensation.

asset_views.thesis: Persistent inflation risk and heavy sovereign supply can keep long-end yields elevated even if near-term policy expectations fluctuate.
asset_views.transmission: Higher inflation compensation and marginal-investor supply absorption needs raise long-end term compensation.
drivers: US debt supply and investor absorption constraints remain a structural concern.
risks: A sequence of benign inflation releases could support duration.
A sharp growth slowdown could overwhelm supply concerns.
asset_views.invalidation_condition: Sustained broad-based disinflation accompanied by falling long-end yields.

evidence.text: US core PCE inflation was 3.3% year over year in July.
Government debt volume and marginal investor demand are identified as drivers of higher required yields.

counterevidence.text: US Treasury yields rolled over slightly after recent highs, according to Saxo.

asset_views.thesis: Energy remains supported by supply disruption and positive carry, but the path is highly dependent on geopolitical normalization.
asset_views.transmission: Tight prompt supply raises spot prices and backwardation, supporting total returns while worsening inflation pressure.
drivers: Low product inventories and strong refinery margins.
risks: Demand deterioration from tighter financial conditions.
asset_views.catalyst: Changes in Gulf shipping and energy supply conditions.
asset_views.invalidation_condition: Energy curves flatten materially or move into contango as physical tightness eases.

evidence.text: Brent and WTI were reported in steep backwardation, with positive one-year implied roll yields.
The Fed study finds futures outperform simple alternatives when curves deviate materially, but remain biased forecasts during high uncertainty.

counterevidence.text: Oil prices steadied after a recent rally, and future spot prices remain difficult to forecast during geopolitical shocks.
counterevidence.evidence_family: 3 September commodity session; Commodity futures forecasting study

asset_views.thesis: The dollar has conditional support from US inflation and policy risk, but broad dollar direction is not established by the supplied evidence.
asset_views.transmission: Relative policy expectations support USD; synchronized growth and non-US tightening can offset that support.
drivers: Fed policy remains conditional on inflation.
Global growth is described as relatively synchronized.
JPY-specific intervention and repricing distort broad FX interpretation.
risks: Renewed non-US policy tightening or intervention effects.
asset_views.invalidation_condition: US inflation cools while non-US central banks retain or increase tightening bias.

evidence.text: Waller said a hot August inflation reading could justify a September rate hike.

counterevidence.text: J.P. Morgan describes synchronized global cyclical resilience as supportive for EM carry and not necessarily a US-exceptionalism regime.
counterevidence.evidence_family: EM FX and global cyclical outlook

asset_views.confidence_rationale: Code-calibrated evidence strength: 1 cited document(s) from 1 conservatively independent evidence family/families from 1 publisher(s); strongest tier is market_interpretation. Explicit counterevidence reduces the displayed tier.
asset_views.thesis: The yen may retain support if higher Japanese short-rate expectations and institutional demand persist, but intervention-driven moves are unstable.
asset_views.transmission: A more hawkish BoJ path narrows rate differentials; official intervention can amplify the move but does not establish durability.
asset_views.catalyst: BoJ communication and the September policy meeting.
asset_views.invalidation_condition: The yen rally reverses as global yields rise and Japanese policy expectations soften.

evidence.text: Saxo reports a sharp yen rally alongside higher Japanese short-rate expectations and a fully priced 25-basis-point hike for the September 18 BoJ meeting.

counterevidence.text: Saxo notes that only one comparable yen sell-off since 2025 held for more than three trading days.

scenarios.description: Inflation remains uneven; central banks retain a conditional tightening bias while growth stays resilient.
signposts: US inflation shows progress but remains above target.
Energy prices remain elevated without a new extreme supply shock.
Long-end yields remain sensitive to supply.

cross_asset_consequences.implication: Duration remains volatile and vulnerable at the long end.
Energy retains support while physical tightness persists.
Valuation-sensitive sectors remain exposed to real-rate volatility.

assumptions.text: US activity and employment remain broadly solid.
Energy-to-core inflation pass-through remains incomplete but becomes a larger risk over time.
assumptions.evidence_family: UK inflation propagation; Global inflation monitor

scenarios.description: Inflation cools sufficiently for the Fed and other central banks to defer further tightening, easing pressure on duration and risk assets.
signposts: Several inflation releases continue the disinflation trend.
Energy prices and futures-curve tightness moderate.
Labor-market weakness becomes more visible without a renewed inflation impulse.

cross_asset_consequences.implication: Front-end and long-end yields could decline.
Lower yields would support duration-sensitive equities.
The dollar could lose relative policy support.

assumptions.text: Waller supports holding rates if disinflation continues.

scenarios.description: Energy and goods inflation intensify, forcing additional tightening while sovereign supply keeps long-end yields elevated.
signposts: US core inflation prints materially hotter than recent readings.
Evidence of second-round inflation effects increases.

cross_asset_consequences.implication: Front-end tightening risk and long-end supply pressure increase.
Energy outperforms on physical tightness and carry.
Higher core rates challenge lower-rated issuers and EM financing.

assumptions.text: BoE analysis warns that energy shocks can generate persistent second-round effects and that waiting may create status-quo bias.
Global core goods inflation and energy pass-through firm further.

disagreements.issue: Whether falling headline or conventional inflation measures provide sufficient evidence to ease inflation concern

sides.position: Disinflation is progressing and labor-market slack may contain persistence.

evidence.text: Waller cites falling three-month core inflation and productivity-adjusted wage growth consistent with continued disinflation.
The Riksbank sees no clear lasting broad inflation upturn and notes labor-market slack.

sides.position: Energy shocks may generate delayed and persistent second-round effects.

evidence.text: Pill argues that UK second-round effects may be stronger than standard models imply and that the MPC should not wait for uncertainty to resolve.
J.P. Morgan expects modest further core-inflation firming as goods and energy pressures offset softer services.

disagreements.resolution_signal: Subsequent core-inflation releases, wage data and evidence of energy pass-through into services and goods inflation.

catalysts.what_matters: Whether inflation continues to improve; Waller would consider holding if it does and hiking if progress reverses.

catalysts.what_matters: Persistence of physical tightness, energy prices and second-round inflation risk.

themes.title: Inflation resilience versus disinflation progress
themes.implication: Rates remain highly data-sensitive; energy-sensitive currencies and inflation hedges may outperform if supply shocks persist, while duration benefits require cleaner inflation evidence.

themes.title: Sovereign supply and market intermediation
themes.implication: Long-duration rates may remain vulnerable even if near-term policy expectations soften; liquidity conditions should be monitored rather than assumed benign.

themes.title: Energy-driven stagflation risk
themes.implication: Favors energy and selected commodity exposure but pressures duration, rate-sensitive equities and non-yielding assets.

themes.title: Fiscal and supply pressure at the long end
themes.implication: Long-end rates remain vulnerable, with knock-on pressure for property, small caps and speculative growth.

themes.title: AI investment remains structurally supported but increasingly selective
themes.implication: Prefer profitable cash generators and energy infrastructure over unprofitable, financing-dependent growth; market confirmation is unavailable.

themes.title: Supply-driven inflation versus restrictive policy
themes.implication: The combination can keep rates higher for longer while weakening real household income and cyclical demand.

themes.title: Global yield and fiscal-risk repricing
themes.implication: The shock is negative for duration and broad risk appetite, but its FX effect is ambiguous where higher yields are interpreted as fiscal rather than monetary strength.

themes.title: AI adoption is broadening, but near-term labour displacement remains limited
themes.implication: The evidence supports gradual labour transformation rather than an immediate employment shock, while investment exposure is more credible through infrastructure and productivity channels than through an assumed aggregate-demand boom.

themes.title: AI investment is becoming a cross-market financing and duration shock
themes.implication: Favourable AI demand does not eliminate financing risk: supply, concentration, leverage and delayed revenue realization can raise credit premia and pressure long-duration assets.
